connections.feedback: Yes. "Best because it's the greatest" says the same thing twice and gives no reason. Asking what makes it the best invites a real reason, and keeps the chat friendly.
Sounding sure is not a reason. The statement went round in a circle, so nothing was actually shown.
Calling Jo biased skips the argument and starts a fight. The problem is in the reasoning, and you can say so politely.
Taste does vary, so "it's all opinion" has some truth. But Jo made a claim about being the best, and you can still ask what they mean by it, which keeps the talk going.
connections.notes: Partly true for taste; ends a conversation that a question could continue.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Yes. Three stories picked out of hundreds may be the best ones. You need to know how they were chosen and what the rest say before they mean anything.
Three is a small number out of hundreds, and success stories are the ones that get shared. The stories alone do not show typical results.
A forum can be wrong, but "unreliable" is too broad a reason to reject. Asking how the stories were picked is fairer and more useful.
Trying it is a form of testing, and you learn about your own case. But one person's short trial says little about whether it generally works, and a diet can carry its own risks.
connections.notes: Personal trial is real evidence for you, weak in general, and may carry costs.

connections.feedback: Yes. Offering only two options hides others, such as smaller cuts, delays or new income. Asking what else exists is the quickest way to test the "no third way" claim.
Looking at the numbers is useful and shows what each option really costs. But it accepts the manager's frame that only these two exist, so better options might never be considered.
connections.notes: Good facts, but works inside a possibly false choice.

connections.feedback: Picking the lesser harm of two sounds sensible, but only if the two really are the only choices. Here that is the thing in doubt.
This accepts the either-or and then decides on a value judgment. The first question is whether there are other ways forward.

connections.feedback: Yes. Experience is worth respecting, but it is not proof about this tool. A failing test is concrete evidence, and inviting the engineer to look at it together keeps the meeting constructive.
Rerunning first avoids a false alarm and spares embarrassment. The cost is time, and if the test is real the group is already moving ahead on the wrong assumption.
connections.notes: Careful and polite; can delay a safety concern.

connections.feedback: Years of experience make a claim more likely to be right, but they do not answer a failing test. Deferring skips the evidence.
Guessing at motives turns a question about a test into a fight about a person. It also makes the evidence harder to discuss.

connections.feedback: Yes. Some feared chains of events are real and some are not. Asking what would link the steps tests the worry, and a short trial with a check point lets evidence decide.
Many slippery-slope arguments are weak, and this one has no evidence offered. But sometimes a chain is real, and brushing the worry aside can lose a chance to watch for it.
connections.notes: Often right about the argument; may ignore a real risk worth monitoring.

connections.feedback: Agreeing to the worry without any reason treats a fear as a fact. Nothing in the claim shows that the chain would happen.
Describing the other side as wanting chaos replaces the argument with a caricature. It makes a calm trial harder to agree on.

sets.label: A price that drops to 25 (teen, introductory)

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Yes. "40" was just the first number you heard, and it can make 25 look like a bargain. Checking what similar games really sell for gives you a fair yardstick.
A big drop from the first price sounds like a gift, but the first price may have been inflated. The drop tells you what the seller started at, not what the game is worth.
Some sellers are fair. Refusing on a rule about all sellers skips finding out whether 25 is a good price.
Haggling can work and it shows you are not accepting the first number. But you are still using the seller's prices to steer your counter-offer, and you do not yet know the real value.
connections.notes: Reasonable tactic; still anchored to the seller's numbers.

connections.feedback: Yes. A feeling tends to collect examples that fit it. Writing down both misses and hits for a few weeks gives you a fair record to judge by.
First impressions can be right, but they are also where bias begins. Trusting it means you stop collecting evidence that could change your mind.
Hearing from people who worked with them adds information. It is second-hand, may carry others' biases, and does not fix your own way of noticing.
connections.notes: Extra information, but second-hand and does not address your own noticing.

connections.feedback: Doubting your impression is healthy, but giving up on forming views is not. The aim is to test it, not to discard judgment.

connections.feedback: Yes. People tend to be too optimistic about their own tasks. Using what similar tasks actually took, and giving a range, is more honest than a single hopeful number.
Doubling a gut feeling is a known rule of thumb and often works. It is crude, gives no range, and hides the reasoning, so a manager cannot judge it.
connections.notes: A useful rule of thumb that hides its reasoning.

connections.feedback: A private buffer protects you, but your manager plans around the number you gave. The cost is an estimate that is not honest to them.
connections.notes: Protects you; the manager plans with a figure you do not believe.

connections.feedback: Three days is the best case, not the likely case. Your own history says tasks like this take longer.

connections.feedback: Yes. Looking at how similar jobs actually went beats trusting a hopeful guess. It pulls you back from the optimism that most of us bring to our own plans.
This uses the best case as if it were the usual case. Past jobs like this took about twice as long.
A doubling rule corrects for optimism roughly. It is better than three days but gives no reason and no range, so it is hard to defend if challenged.
A private buffer protects you, but your manager plans around the number you gave. It also trains you to keep an optimistic gut feeling instead of correcting it.
connections.notes: Protects you; the estimate is not honest to the person relying on it.

connections.feedback: Yes. The six months are spent either way. Asking the team to argue for the remaining work as if starting today keeps the decision about future value, with the new market information included.
A short extension with a firm review gives time to gather facts and limits the exposure. The risk is that a short extension becomes a long one, and the review point must be real.
connections.notes: Reasonable hedge; needs a review point that is actually enforced.

connections.feedback: This is the sunk-cost trap: past effort is spent whichever way you go. It adds more cost to a project whose need has shifted.
Cancelling to send a message is also a decision about the past. The question is whether the remaining work is worth it now.

connections.feedback: Yes. Your investment in the plan makes it hard to read mixed data fairly. Naming in advance what would change your mind makes the review harder to argue away afterward.
Early results really are noisy, so waiting has a basis. The risk is that waiting becomes a way to avoid being challenged, with the team and money committed in the meantime.
connections.notes: True about noisy data; may become a way to avoid challenge.

connections.feedback: A reviewer who understands the plan can give informed comments. A reviewer chosen for knowing the plan may also share your assumptions, so the review is less independent.
Pointing to supportive numbers while skipping the rest is confirmation bias in action. The team deserves the whole picture.
